heroHeadline: Day 15 of MSF Cité Soleil Hospital Closure — 300,000 Residents Without Emergency Care; TPS Supreme Court Ruling Weeks Away as ~350,000 Haitian Holders Await Decision; PM Fils-Aimé: No Electoral Decree Issued, No Registration Begun
heroSubtitle: MSF's Cité Soleil hospital — the only emergency facility for ~300,000 commune residents — entered its 15th consecutive day of closure on May 24, 2026, with gang conditions preventing safe access and no reopening timeline announced. The intra-Viv Ansanm gang war (Chen Mechan/Taliban/400 Mawozo vs. Duvivier/Pyè 6 factions) that forced the May 10 evacuation continues across Cité Soleil and the Cul-de-Sac Plain. Approximately 30,000 people have been displaced since May 10, pushing the total national IDP count to ~1.5 million. OCHA's latest Crisis in Numbers (May 7) documents 6.4 million Haitians (>50% of population) requiring emergency humanitarian assistance in 2026 — a 6.7% increase from 2025 — with the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan ($880M) only ~20% funded ($172M secured), a $708M shortfall. The GSF's ~800-person advance force (400+ Chadian, 75 Guatemalan, 70 Salvadoran; under Mongolian Maj. Gen. Erdenebat Batsuuri since May 14) held a high-level coordination meeting with Haiti's Ministry of Defense on May 23, as the force remains exclusively concentrated in Port-au-Prince city center — leaving Cité Soleil, Artibonite, Centre, and Sud-Est without international security coverage. On the political front, approximately 350,000 Haitian TPS holders in the US await the Supreme Court's ruling in Noem v. Doe / Trump v. Miot — expected late June to early July 2026 — with the Court's conservative majority signaling potential deference to the Trump administration at April 29 oral arguments. PM Fils-Aimé's May 12 abandonment of the August 30 election date (revised target: elections by end-2026, new president by February 2027) stands unrevised; no electoral decree has been issued; voter registration has not begun; 23 communes remain inaccessible. ACLED's May 2026 overview documented a record 38 deaths in Sud-Est — historically low-violence — as gangs expand via 'balloon effect' from GSF-pressured Port-au-Prince zones to regions with no international presence.
